title: WHY GOD WON’T BLESS WHAT YOU WON’T SURRENDER
paragraphs:
WHY GOD WON’T BLESS WHAT YOU WON’T SURRENDER
You keep asking God to put His hand of blessing on it. But what if the very thing you are begging Him to bless is the thing He has been asking you to place in His hands?
There is a prayer almost nobody wants to pray.
Not because the words are difficult.
Because we already know what the answer might cost us.
“Lord… if You want it, You can have it.”
The relationship.
The ambition.
The money.
The secret habit.
The bitterness you have justified for years.
The image you desperately maintain.
The dream you have quietly turned into an idol.
The person you cannot imagine living without.
The version of your future you have already written—and now expect God to sign.
We can spend months asking God to bless something we have never actually surrendered to Him.
We pray over it.
Cry over it.
Fast over it.
Defend it.
Post Bible verses about it.
Ask other people to agree with us about it.
And sometimes, underneath all that spiritual language, there is a frighteningly simple truth:
We do not really want God’s will.
We want God’s approval of ours.
That distinction can expose the soul.
Because Jesus Christ did not come merely to become another addition to the life you already planned.
He came as Lord.
And sooner or later, every disciple reaches an altar where Jesus touches something precious and asks the question we would rather avoid:
“Do you trust Me with this too?”
Maybe that is why these words are finding you right now.
Maybe there is something you have been asking God to bless while quietly refusing to let Him govern it.
And before you read another paragraph, understand this clearly:
God’s grace cannot be purchased by surrender.
We are not saved because we surrendered enough, sacrificed enough, cried enough, served enough, donated enough, shared enough, or behaved well enough.
Salvation is the gift of God through Jesus Christ.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8).
The cross destroys every attempt to bargain with God.
You cannot place something on the altar and then hand God an invoice.
You cannot say, “I surrendered this, therefore You owe me that.”
God owes us nothing.
Yet in Christ, He has given sinners what we could never earn: mercy, reconciliation, forgiveness, adoption, eternal life.
That makes surrender even more beautiful.
Christian surrender is not payment for grace.
It is a response to grace.
Paul writes in Romans 12:1:
Notice the order.
Mercy first.
Sacrifice second.
God’s mercy produces surrender.
Surrender does not purchase God’s mercy.

That distinction matters because Christianity is not a transaction in which we give God enough obedience until He gives us the house, spouse, promotion, healing, business, platform, money, or comfortable future we requested.
Sometimes surrender leads to receiving.
Sometimes surrender leads to losing.
Sometimes God returns Isaac.
Sometimes He allows Paul’s thorn to remain.
Sometimes the prison doors open.
Sometimes Stephen sees heaven open while stones are still falling.
The ultimate blessing of surrender is not getting everything you wanted.
It is getting Christ.
And perhaps that is exactly where your heart has been struggling.
You want Jesus.
But you also want control.
You want His presence.
But you want veto power.
You want Him to lead—as long as He leads where you already intended to go.
Jesus never disguised the cost of discipleship.
Mark 8:34 records His words:
“Whosoever will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.”
The Greek carries the force of the statement.
ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτὸν — aparnēsasthō heauton
“Let him deny himself.”
This is stronger than denying yourself a temporary pleasure.
Jesus is not merely describing skipping dessert, deleting an app, or giving something up for a few weeks.
The call reaches the throne of the self.
The self that says:
“My life belongs to me.”
“My body belongs to me.”
“My money belongs to me.”
“My sexuality belongs to me.”
“My future belongs to me.”
“My reputation belongs to me.”
“My revenge belongs to me.”
“My dreams belong to me.”
“My decisions belong to me.”
Jesus walks directly toward that throne.
Not because He hates you.
Because He intends to save you from a ruler who was never capable of saving you:
yourself.
Then He says:
ἀράτω τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ — aratō ton stauron autou
“Let him take up his cross.”
We have domesticated the cross.
We hang it around our necks.
Place it on walls.
Print it on shirts.
Put it in church logos.
But the people who first heard Jesus speak did not think of jewelry.
They thought of death.
Humiliation.
Execution.
No return to the old life.
Jesus was calling people to something infinitely deeper than religious improvement.
He was calling them to die to self-rule and follow Him.
And then He said something astonishing:
“For whosoever will save his life shall lose it; but whosoever shall lose his life for my sake and the gospel’s, the same shall save it” (Mark 8:35).
There is the paradox at the heart of surrender.
What you clutch can become your prison.
What you surrender to Christ can no longer be your god.
Read that again.
What you surrender to Christ can no longer be your god.
Maybe the thing hurting you most is not simply what happened to you.
Maybe it is what you refuse to release.
You are still carrying the betrayal.
Still replaying the conversation.
Still checking their profile.
Still fantasizing about proving them wrong.
Still building your identity around somebody who left.
Still feeding a private addiction while asking God for public influence.
Still compromising in a relationship because loneliness feels scarier than disobedience.
Still measuring your worth by money.
Still telling yourself that when you finally become successful, attractive, married, wealthy, recognized, healed, or admired, then you will finally be enough.
And Jesus stands before all of it.
Not with hatred.
Not with sadistic delight in taking things away.
With nail-scarred hands.
That changes everything.
The One asking you to surrender is the One who gave Himself for you.
Jesus is not asking you to walk a road He refused to walk.
Gethsemane proves it.
There, under crushing anguish, Jesus prayed:
“Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done” (Luke 22:42).
Read those final words slowly.
πλὴν μὴ τὸ θέλημά μου ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν γινέσθω
“Nevertheless, not my will, but Yours be done.”
This was not passive resignation.
This was holy surrender.

And we must be careful here: Jesus was not surrendering sinful desires. He was the sinless Son of God. He was willingly submitting Himself to the Father’s redemptive purpose, going toward the cross where He would bear sin for sinners.
The scandal of Christianity is not merely that God asks for surrender.
It is that before He asked you to give Him your life, Christ gave His life for you.
The King became a servant.
The Holy One was mocked.
The Innocent One was condemned.
The Creator was struck by creatures whose lungs were filling with air He provided.
Hands He formed drove nails through His hands.
Human mouths He created spat upon Him.
And He continued toward Calvary.
Why?
Because sinners needed more than motivation.
We needed redemption.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin.
He suffered.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
Christianity is not the story of broken people becoming impressive enough for God.
It is the story of a holy God showing astonishing grace to people who could never rescue themselves.
That means surrender is not walking toward an executioner hoping He will tolerate you.
It is falling into the hands of the Savior who was crucified for you.
Still, surrender hurts.
Ask Abraham.
Genesis 22 contains one of Scripture’s most unsettling tests.
God calls:
“Abraham.”
And Abraham responds:
הִנֵּנִי — hinnēnî
“Here I am.”
Those words are beautiful until God touches Isaac.
The son of promise.
The child Abraham waited years to hold.
The future he thought he understood.
Suddenly “Here I am” was no longer religious vocabulary.
It had weight.
Because surrender becomes real when God touches what you love.
It is easy to sing, “I surrender all,” while imagining that “all” means everything except that.
But the altar reveals what songs can hide.
Abraham obeyed, and God stopped him from sacrificing Isaac. God provided the ram.
Yet Genesis 22 is not a formula promising that if you surrender something, God must return it in a better package.
Its ultimate trajectory points beyond Abraham.
Toward another beloved Son.
A Son who would not be spared.
Jesus.
At Calvary there would be no ram taking His place.
Christ Himself would be the sacrifice.
This is why the Gospel reaches places motivational religion never can.
The Gospel does not merely say:
“Give something up.”
It says:
“Look at what Christ gave to redeem you.”
And suddenly repentance is no longer merely losing something.
It is turning from what is killing you toward the One who died to give you life.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that means.
There is a name in your mind right now.
A habit.
A relationship.
A compromise.
An account.
A private conversation.
A hidden browser history.
A grudge.
A plan.
An obsession.
Something you would be terrified to hear Jesus ask you to release.
Do not rush past that discomfort.
Sit there for a moment.
Because sometimes we call something a “blessing” simply because we desperately want it.
But desire does not determine holiness.
Opportunity does not equal permission.
Chemistry does not equal covenant.
Profit does not equal God’s approval.
Popularity does not equal anointing.
An open door is not automatically a door God opened.
And getting what you prayed for is not necessarily proof that God endorsed every choice that brought you there.
Scripture refuses to reduce blessing to comfort.
Psalm 1 calls the person who delights in God’s instruction blessed.
Jesus calls the poor in spirit blessed.
He calls those who mourn blessed.
He calls the meek blessed.
He calls those who hunger and thirst after righteousness blessed.
He even calls those persecuted for righteousness’ sake blessed.
Biblical blessing is far deeper than getting your preferred circumstances.
Sometimes the blessing is that God refuses to let your idol satisfy you.
Sometimes mercy feels like disruption.
Sometimes love sounds like conviction.
Sometimes God’s rescue begins when the thing you thought you could never live without starts losing its grip on you.
Think about the rich young ruler.
He came running to Jesus.
He had morality.
Respectability.
Possessions.
Religious seriousness.
Mark tells us something profoundly important before Jesus confronted his deepest attachment:
“Then Jesus beholding him loved him…” (Mark 10:21).
Loved him.
Do not miss that.
Jesus’ hard word came from love.
Christ identified the place where the man’s possessions possessed him.
Then came the invitation:
“…come, take up the cross, and follow me.”
And the man walked away sorrowful.
He came close enough to hear Jesus.
Close enough to be loved by Jesus.
Close enough to receive the invitation.
But something else had his heart.
That story should frighten every comfortable Christian.
Because it is possible to want eternal life while resisting the lordship of Christ.
It is possible to admire Jesus while refusing to follow Him into the one room of your life you keep locked.
We should not twist this passage into a simplistic claim that every Christian must dispose of every possession. Scripture addresses wealth in more nuanced ways than that.
But we should absolutely allow the passage to ask its intended heart-level question:
What possesses you?
What could Jesus ask for that would make you walk away sad?
There.
That may be your altar.
And perhaps you have been asking:
“Why won’t God bless this?”
But another question may be more revealing:
“Why am I so afraid to surrender it?”
Because if losing something would make you abandon Jesus, that thing may already occupy a place in your heart that belongs to Him.
This does not mean every loss is caused by idolatry.
It does not mean suffering automatically proves hidden sin.
Job demolishes that simplistic theology.
The man born blind in John 9 demolishes it too.
We must never look at another suffering person and casually declare, “God took that because you wouldn’t surrender.”
That can be cruel, presumptuous, and biblically irresponsible.
We do not know every purpose of God.
But Scripture does give us permission to examine our own hearts.
“Search me, O God, and know my heart…” (Psalm 139:23).
So this message is not ammunition for judging somebody else.
It is a mirror.
What are you protecting from Jesus?
Maybe you have been saying:
“God, bless my relationship.”
But you know the relationship continually pulls you toward sin.
“God, bless my business.”
But you are cutting ethical corners.
“God, bless my finances.”
But money already determines your identity and security.
“God, bless my ministry.”
But secretly you need applause more than you need holiness.
“God, restore my marriage.”
But you refuse to confess, forgive, seek help, change destructive behavior, or practice costly love.
“God, use me.”
But you refuse to repent privately.
“God, give me peace.”
But you keep feeding the very thing destroying your peace.
There are moments when the prayer must change.
From:
“God, make this work.”
To:
“God, make me Yours.”
From:
“God, give me what I want.”
To:
“God, teach me to want what pleases You.”
From:
“God, remove every consequence.”
To:
“God, transform my heart.”
From:
“God, bless my plans.”
To:
“Jesus, You are Lord. Rewrite them if You must.”
That prayer is terrifying.
Because He might.
But here is what fear forgets:
You are not surrendering to a stranger.
You are surrendering to Jesus.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who wept.
The One who forgave.
The One who restored Peter after Peter publicly denied Him.
Peter’s story is exactly why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to one theme:
Peter had boasted that he would never fall away.
Hours later, he was denying that he even knew Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Imagine that sound.
Imagine Peter realizing that the man who had sworn loyalty had become the man Jesus said he would become.
Luke records that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
Scandal.
Failure.
Shame.
The kind of moment you think should become the final paragraph of your story.
But Jesus was not finished writing.
After the resurrection, John 21 brings Peter back beside a charcoal fire.
That detail matters.
John 18 tells us there had also been a charcoal fire when Peter denied Jesus.
Imagine what the smell might have awakened in him.
Memory.
Failure.
Shame.
And now Jesus brings Peter into another moment beside another charcoal fire.
Not to humiliate him.
To restore him.
“Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?”
Again.
Again.
Again.
Three denials.
Three questions.
Then:
“Feed my sheep.”
Jesus did not pretend Peter’s failure never happened.
Grace did something better.
Grace met Peter inside the wreckage and rewrote what failure had tried to make final.
That is the Gospel.
Not pretending sin does not matter.
Not calling rebellion freedom.
Not renaming darkness so nobody feels uncomfortable.
Grace confronts sin precisely because grace intends to rescue sinners from it.
Jesus does not merely forgive you in your chains.
He begins transforming you so the chains no longer define you.
That is why surrender matters.
You cannot cling to the prison and complain that Jesus has not led you into freedom.
You cannot enthrone the idol and ask Christ to decorate its temple.
You cannot knowingly cherish rebellion and call His conviction rejection.
But neither should you imagine that surrender makes you worthy of love.
Christ loved first.
“We love him, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).
Maybe you failed last night.
Maybe you fell again.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
Maybe your Bible has highlights everywhere while your heart has a locked room nobody is allowed to enter.
Maybe you lead others while privately wondering whether God could possibly still want you.
Hear the Gospel clearly:
Stop hiding.
Come to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Not because sin is small.
Because Christ is sufficient.
The blood of Jesus is not permission to remain comfortably enslaved to sin.
Grace teaches us to turn from ungodliness.
The Jesus who says, “Neither do I condemn thee,” also says, “go, and sin no more” (John 8:11).
Grace and repentance are not enemies.
Grace makes repentance possible.
And perhaps your surrender begins with three words:
“Jesus, take it.”
Not because the words themselves are magical.
Because the heart has finally stopped negotiating.
Take my reputation.
Take my future.
Take this relationship if it dishonors You.
Take this addiction—I cannot defeat it without You.
Take my resentment.
Take my need to be admired.
Take my plans.
Take my money.
Take my sexuality.
Take my success.
Take my failure.
Take the version of myself I have been desperately trying to protect.
Forgive my sin.
Rule my life.
Teach me obedience.
Make me more like You.
And if surrender means I do not receive the outcome I wanted…
be enough for me anyway.
That final sentence separates biblical surrender from prosperity religion.
Jesus is not a vending machine.
Christianity is not inserting obedience until a blessing falls out.
God may give.
God may withhold.
God may redirect.
God may close a door.
God may open one you never imagined.
God may answer immediately.
God may teach you to wait.
And sometimes, like Paul pleading over his thorn, you may hear an answer different from the one you wanted:
“My grace is sufficient for thee…” (2 Corinthians 12:9).
Sometimes the answer is not escape.
Sometimes the answer is sufficient grace.
And grace can carry a surrendered person where comfort never could.
Be real.

And if Christ has already delivered you from something you once thought you could never surrender, tell that testimony. Somebody scrolling through those comments may need evidence that grace still rebuilds lives.
Not because saving a post earns anything from God.
It does not.
Sharing Christian content does not make anyone righteous before God. Supporting a ministry does not purchase blessing, salvation, answered prayer, or a better place in heaven.
Only Christ saves.

But if Gospel-centered truth has helped you, supporting its continued spread can be one practical way of participating in the work of placing biblical encouragement before more people. If you want to glorify God through the resources He has entrusted to you, consider whether supporting and sharing faithful Gospel work is one of the ways you can serve others—not from guilt, not as payment for blessing, but freely, prayerfully, and for His glory.
But before you leave, there is one final question.
Not for the comments.
Not for your friends.
Not for the person you wish had read this.
For you.
What are you still holding?
You have prayed about it.
Protected it.
Explained it.
Excused it.
Cried over it.
Maybe even asked God repeatedly to bless it.
But have you surrendered it?
Jesus asked a devastating question immediately after calling His followers to deny themselves:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (Mark 8:36).
The Greek word translated “profit” is ὠφελεῖ — ōphelei.
What does it benefit?
What does it actually gain you?
That question still cuts through every generation.
What does it profit you to win the relationship and lose your obedience?
To build the platform and lose your integrity?
To accumulate the money and lose your worship?
To protect the secret and lose your peace?
To prove them wrong and become bitter?
To gain everybody’s applause while becoming spiritually hollow?
To hold the whole world in your hands while refusing to place your heart in the hands of Christ?
One day, everything you are clutching will leave your hands anyway.
The career.
The house.
The account.
The reputation.
The trophies.
The followers.
The body.
The applause.
The plans.
Everything.
But Jesus Christ remains.
So surrender is not God trying to empty your hands merely for the sake of emptiness.
It is the invitation to stop treating temporary things as though they can carry the eternal weight of your soul.
Open your hands.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Seek forgiveness where you have sinned.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Get accountable if secrecy has been feeding your bondage.
Walk away from what Christ calls sin.
And where the issue is not sinful but simply precious, hold it with open hands before God.
Then pray without bargaining:

“Father, because of Your mercy, I give this to You. If it should remain, let it remain under Your lordship. If it should go, keep my heart faithful. If You redirect me, teach me to follow. If You make me wait, teach me to trust. Forgive my sins through Jesus Christ. Break every idol I have placed above You. I do not want merely Your gifts while resisting Your rule. I want Christ. Your will be done.”
Maybe your scandal is real.
Maybe the screenshots exist.
Maybe the marriage is wounded.
Maybe the addiction has left scars.
Maybe your children know what happened.
Maybe the church knows.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you destroyed something you cannot rebuild by yourself.
Maybe your greatest shame has already happened.
Peter had his rooster.
Thomas had his doubt.
Paul had his history.
The thief had his cross.
And sinners like us have ours.
Yet none of those stories places human failure above the authority of Jesus Christ to save.
The Gospel does not promise that every earthly consequence disappears.
It promises something infinitely greater:
There is grace for repentant sinners in Jesus.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is resurrection after the tomb.
There is a Savior stronger than your shame.
There is a King worthy of the thing you are terrified to surrender.
So share this with somebody carrying something too heavy to keep pretending about.
Because maybe the thing you are terrified to place in His hands is the very thing keeping your hands too full to cling completely to Him.
The altar is not where your story dies. In the hands of Jesus, it may be where the lie that ruled your story finally does.
